questions.question: Which responsibility belongs to Elasticsearch rather than Kibana?
options: Arranging dashboard panels
Storing and indexing source documents and executing aggregations
Copying saved objects between spaces
Rendering a Lens visualization
questions.explanation: Elasticsearch stores and indexes the source data, executes searches, and computes aggregations. Kibana builds the experience and renders the returned evidence.

questions.question: What does a KQL expression do by itself?
options: Filters documents that match its conditions
Sorts documents by relevance
Computes percentiles and cardinality
Changes the underlying index mapping
questions.explanation: KQL is a filtering language. It does not aggregate, transform, or sort data; those operations are expressed elsewhere and executed by Elasticsearch.

questions.question: A dashboard has `log.level: error`, a production filter pill, and a one-hour time range. Which documents should its panels use?
options: Every error document regardless of time or environment
Every production document from the last hour
Only documents satisfying the KQL, pill, and time constraints together
Only documents cached in the browser
questions.explanation: The query, structured filters, and time filter form one effective evidence scope. Each constraint narrows the documents available to the panels.

questions.question: A user can open a dashboard in its Kibana space, but every panel receives a forbidden response. What should be checked next?
options: Whether the role can read the underlying Elasticsearch indices
Whether the dashboard has a darker color theme
Whether the user exported the dashboard yesterday
Whether KQL supports sorting
questions.explanation: Kibana feature access and Elasticsearch data access are separate. Dashboard read access does not grant read privileges on the source indices.

questions.question: How should a dashboard be promoted when it depends on visualizations and a data view?
options: Copy only the dashboard line from the NDJSON file
Recreate every dependent object manually in production
Export the dashboard with its reference graph and treat the NDJSON as opaque
Write the dashboard directly into a source-data index
questions.explanation: Kibana's export API can include deep references. The resulting NDJSON is a versioned, opaque artifact and should not be hand-edited.

questions.question: A scheduled rule finds matching data, but its connector has been deleted. Which outcome is most accurate?
options: No alert state can exist because notification delivery is the rule condition
The alert can be created or updated, while the connector action fails
Elasticsearch automatically recreates the connector
The dashboard role gains connector management privileges
questions.explanation: Rule evaluation, alert state, and action delivery are distinct. A deleted connector can prevent the action even when the condition was evaluated and alert state exists.

questions.question: Why is a quiet notification channel insufficient evidence that the monitored system stayed healthy?
options: Kibana never runs scheduled work
A Task Manager delay or connector failure can create an evaluation or delivery gap
KQL ignores all time filters
Saved objects are stored only in the browser
questions.explanation: A rule can run late, fail to evaluate, or fail to deliver its action. Monitor rule execution and connector health instead of treating no notification as proof of no incident.
